questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion and the observable behind it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the observable behind a stated criterion
questions.stem: A planning memo scores 'good legibility of the street' without saying what a marker should look at when applying it.

options.text: Treat the criterion as incomplete, because it names a quality without pointing to anything a marker can observe.
Treat the criterion as complete, because experienced markers will all know what legibility means.
options.misconception: assumes shared professional judgement fills the gap

options.text: Add a score band from zero to five, since the numbers will make the criterion precise.
options.misconception: believes a numeric scale supplies the missing observable

options.text: Ask applicants to explain how legible their street is, and score their explanation.
options.misconception: treats the applicant's own claim as the observable

questions.explanation: A criterion is usable when it points to something a marker can see in the submission, and this one points to nothing. Shared experience may fill the gap on one panel and on another, so the gap has to be closed in writing.
questions.hint: Ask what a marker would look at on the drawing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rubric level describes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a rubric level actually specifies
questions.stem: A memo's scoring sheet has bands labelled 'weak, adequate, good, strong' for design quality, and the officer asks what each band is supposed to describe.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a rubric band describes the quality of performance against a stated criterion, not the criterion itself and not the mark to be awarded. The bands work only if each one names the features of the submission that would place it there, so 'good' has to say what in the drawings or the written scheme earns that band, otherwise two markers will use the same word for different things.

questions.explanation: A band names the quality of performance against a criterion, so it has to say what in the submission places it there. Without that, the same word is applied to different work by different markers.
questions.hint: Ask what in the submission earns the band.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Improvement as the thing being marked
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish improvement from mere compliance in marking

stimulus.body: The panel is asked to score this year's housing scheme on how much it improves on the 2019 approval. The paper lists the 2019 scheme's unit numbers and storey heights but does not describe its street frontage.

questions.stem: Which step makes the improvement judgement workable for the panel?

options.text: Score the scheme on its own merits, since every panel should be free of the history of a site.
options.misconception: treats a missing baseline as a reason for no comparison

options.text: Describe the 2019 scheme's relevant features first, so the panel can see what the improvement consists of.
Ask the applicant to state how their scheme improves on the previous approval.
options.misconception: accepts the applicant's own account as the baseline

options.text: Average the panel's scores with the 2019 score, to reflect the change over time.
options.misconception: mixes two incompatible scales into a single number

questions.explanation: Improvement is a comparison, so the earlier scheme has to be described in the same terms the new one will be judged in. Asking the applicant to make the case for their own improvement, or averaging two scales, produces a preference rather than a finding.
questions.hint: Ask what the 2019 scheme was like, in writing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet
questions.stem: A city design code requires every application to demonstrate that its scheme contains no bicycle parking at all, and no submission in the recent batch can meet that.

options.text: Award the point automatically, since it is a published requirement of the design code.
options.misconception: assumes a published criterion must be satisfiable

options.text: Award half a point to every application, since the requirement is at least part of the code.
options.misconception: spreads a defective criterion so that nobody is penalised

options.text: Treat the criterion as unmeetable, because it excludes every case and cannot separate the submissions.
Score the criterion on how well the applicant argues the requirement in its covering letter.
options.misconception: scores the argument rather than the submission

questions.explanation: A criterion that no submission can meet awards nobody anything and its weight falls silently on the other criteria. Recognising it as unmeetable is what allows the officer to report the effect on the ranking rather than publish a distorted result.
questions.hint: Ask whether the criterion can separate two applications.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion every submission meets
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that every submission meets
questions.stem: A committee memo asks panels to score 'confirmation that the site address is given in the application', and every application in the batch gives an address.

options.text: Award the point to every applicant, since the requirement is met and the point is on the sheet.
options.misconception: keeps a non-discriminating point because the points are there

options.text: Award half the point to applicants whose address matches the site plan exactly.
options.misconception: invents a finer test to justify a point that discriminates nothing

options.text: Remove the point from all applications, since it was not earned by anyone in the batch.
options.misconception: treats a met criterion as an unearned one

options.text: Note the criterion as met by all and give it no weight, because it cannot tell the applicants apart.

questions.explanation: A criterion that every submission meets carries no information about quality, and keeping its marks inflates every total by the same amount. Recording it as met by all and giving it no weight leaves the ranking to the criteria that discriminate.
questions.hint: Ask what the point would separate between applicants.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: Work out what a set of weightings rewards
questions.stem: A scoring matrix gives 60 per cent of the total to five design criteria and 40 per cent to five transport criteria, and the committee asks what the matrix rewards.

options.text: It rewards design quality far more heavily than transport, so a strong design can outscore weaker design with better transport.
It rewards nothing in particular, because the criteria are weighted in proportion to their importance.
options.misconception: assumes a weighting scheme must reflect the panel's own priorities

options.text: It rewards balanced submissions, because every criterion still carries some marks.
options.misconception: reads the presence of weights as if all criteria counted equally

options.text: It rewards large schemes, because the criteria marked highest are the ones large schemes usually meet.
options.misconception: assumes weightings track what certain kinds of scheme do well

questions.explanation: Weightings are priorities expressed in marks, and with 60 per cent on design the totals will follow the design scores much more closely than the transport ones. A matrix therefore rewards a particular shape of performance, and applicants can be expected to aim at it.
questions.hint: Ask which criterion can compensate for weakness in the other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Self-assessment without a shared reference point
questions.learningObjective: Explain why self-assessment needs a shared reference point
questions.stem: A design panel asks each applicant to self-assess its scheme against the code before the panel reads it, and the self-assessments range from 40 to 92 per cent.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the self-assessments measure the applicants' reading of the code rather than the schemes' quality, because each applicant applied its own idea of what the bands meant. Without a shared reference point, such as one worked example scored by the panel, a spread of 40 to 92 says more about the readers than about the designs, and the panel should treat the figures as uninformative until calibration has been added.

questions.explanation: Self-assessment without a shared reference measures each applicant's own reading rather than the scheme it describes. A calibrated worked example is what makes the numbers comparable, and without it the spread says little about design quality.
questions.hint: Ask what the applicants were reading as the same standard.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Scores that follow a relationship rather than a text
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a score that tracks a relationship rather than a text

stimulus.body: A panel's notes record that every scheme over 4,000 square metres of retail floor space scored below 9 out of 15 on public realm quality, and every smaller scheme scored above 9.

questions.stem: The officer notices this pattern in the notes. What does it suggest, and what should be done?

options.text: The notes show that large schemes are inherently of lower quality, so the pattern is a genuine finding to report.
options.misconception: reads a scoring artefact as a property of large schemes

options.text: Check whether the panel's reading of the quality descriptors differs by size, since the scores may track size rather than the text.
Adjust every large scheme's score upward to match the small ones, so the panel treats all sizes alike.
options.misconception: corrects a possible bias by imposing an assumption

options.text: Discard the notes and rescore the batch without the area information, to remove the effect.
options.misconception: removes the record instead of testing the pattern

questions.explanation: A clean split by size across every scheme is more likely to be the measurement showing through than a fact about large developments. Checking the descriptors and the markers' assumptions is what tells the officer which of the two she is looking at.
questions.hint: Ask whether the descriptors mention size at all.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion and the observable behind it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the observable behind a stated criterion
questions.stem: A memo's criterion reads 'the design should demonstrate consideration of the site's heritage assets', and markers are asked what to look for.

options.text: Ask each applicant to attest that heritage has been considered, and record the attestation with the score.
options.misconception: accepts a declaration in place of an observable

options.text: Ask markers to apply their professional judgement about heritage, as the code has always done.
options.misconception: leaves the criterion without an observable to check

options.text: Point to the observable in the submission, such as a heritage statement identifying assets and their effects.
Replace the criterion with a requirement for a heritage impact assessment, adding a new document.
options.misconception: changes the submission requirement rather than the criterion

questions.explanation: A criterion becomes usable when it points to a thing in the submission, and here that thing is the heritage statement and what it shows. Changing the submission requirement instead leaves the criterion exactly as uncheckable as before.
questions.hint: Ask which document would show the consideration.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rubric level describes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a rubric level actually specifies
questions.stem: A panel's rubric for a criterion about open space has bands 'basic, good, generous', and a marker asks what 'generous' is meant to require.

options.text: The number of marks to be awarded, so that the panel can total the scores quickly.
options.misconception: confuses a band with the mark attached to it

options.text: The size of the applicant's design team, since bigger teams deliver better public space.
options.misconception: reads a quality band as a statement about resources

options.text: The presence of a landscape plan, which is the document that proves the open space exists.
options.misconception: confuses the evidence of a performance with the performance itself

options.text: The amount and quality of open space provided relative to the scheme, as a description of performance.

questions.explanation: A band describes the quality of performance at that level, in terms of what the submission provides, so that another marker could place the same scheme in the same band. Marks, team size and document lists are not descriptions of performance at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a second marker would need to see to agree.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Improvement as the thing being marked
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish improvement from mere compliance in marking
questions.stem: A city asks panels to judge a new bus corridor design on the improvement it brings over the existing one, and the officer asks how the assessment should be set up.

options.text: Specify the existing conditions the design is measured against, so the improvement becomes a comparison between two stated things.
Ask the applicant to describe the improvement in their design and access statement.
options.misconception: relies on the applicant's account of the comparison

options.text: Assess the new design on its own merits, because an existing corridor is a poor benchmark.
options.misconception: avoids comparison instead of specifying it

options.text: Compare the new design with the best scheme the panel has seen, to set a fair bar.
options.misconception: sets a moving benchmark the existing corridor cannot supply

questions.explanation: Judging improvement requires the earlier condition to be stated, because improvement is a difference between two things. Without that, the panel is comparing a drawing with an impression and the judgment becomes a preference.
questions.hint: Ask what the corridor is being compared against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet
questions.stem: A development brief's assessment includes a criterion awarding marks for the removal of all mature trees on the site, and the city has confirmed that no application can meet it.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a criterion that no submission can meet cannot discriminate, because every application loses the same marks and the score is decided by the other criteria alone. The defensible response is to record the defect, report the consequence for the batch's ranking, and refer the wording back for correction, so the published brief and the marks awarded are reconciled rather than quietly left in place.

questions.explanation: A criterion no submission can meet separates nobody and silently distorts the ranking by its weight. Recording the defect and referring the wording back keeps the published brief and the marks awarded in step.
questions.hint: Ask what the criterion does to the ranking of the batch.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion every submission meets
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that every submission meets

stimulus.body: A committee's assessment sheet has one row for 'whether the application form was signed and dated'. All 14 submissions in the batch are signed and dated, and the sheet gives this row two points.

questions.stem: The committee asks what to do with that row before the scores are totalled.

options.text: Award the marks to all 14 submissions, since the requirement is a published condition of the process.
options.misconception: keeps a non-discriminating row because the requirement is real

options.text: Mark the row as met by all and award it no discriminating weight, so the total reflects what separates the submissions.
Award the marks only to the three submissions with the most legible signatures.
options.misconception: invents a legibility test to justify marks nobody can earn

options.text: Remove the row and report the batch's scores on the remaining criteria only, without comment.
options.misconception: changes the assessment without recording the change

questions.explanation: Points that every applicant receives raise every total equally and change no ranking, while inflating the numbers in a published score sheet. Recording the row as met and giving it no weight keeps the total informative about the submissions.
questions.hint: Ask what the two points would separate between applicants.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: Work out what a set of weightings rewards
questions.stem: A matrix weights site context at 5 per cent, affordable housing delivery at 30 per cent and design at 65 per cent, and a member asks what the matrix rewards.

options.text: It rewards nothing in particular, because the weights were set by the committee itself.
options.misconception: assumes official weightings must be neutral in effect

options.text: It rewards schemes on large sites, because the design weight is the one large schemes usually meet.
options.misconception: assumes weightings track what certain kinds of scheme do well

options.text: It rewards design most, so a scheme with strong design and modest housing delivery can outscore a weaker design.
It rewards balanced schemes, because a low-weighted criterion still counts for something.
options.misconception: reads the presence of weights as if all criteria counted equally

questions.explanation: With 65 per cent of the marks on design, the totals will track design scores closely, and weakness in housing delivery can be outweighed by design. The matrix is a statement of priorities, and it should be defended as one rather than read as a neutral measurement.
questions.hint: Ask which criterion can outweigh the others.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Self-assessment without a shared reference point
questions.learningObjective: Explain why self-assessment needs a shared reference point
questions.stem: A panel asks two applicant teams to self-score the same scheme and one returns 50 per cent while the other returns 88 per cent.

options.text: Average the two self-scores to get a fair figure for the scheme they scored.
options.misconception: averages away the calibration problem

options.text: Ask the teams to explain their scoring and accept the one that seems better reasoned.
options.misconception: treats the quality of the argument as a substitute for a shared standard

options.text: Use the higher self-score as the starting point, since ambition is part of design quality.
options.misconception: rewards confidence in place of calibration

options.text: Treat the gap as evidence about the two teams' readings, and calibrate with a worked example first.

questions.explanation: The same scheme scored 50 by one team and 88 by another shows the two are measuring with different standards, not that the scheme sits in between. A worked example scored by the panel gives the teams a reference point that their own precedents cannot supply.
questions.hint: Ask what the two teams were each reading as the standard.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Scores that follow a relationship rather than a text
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a score that tracks a relationship rather than a text
questions.stem: A panel's notes show that scores for 'landscape quality' rise steadily with the area of communal garden provided, across all 20 schemes assessed.

options.text: Treat the relationship as a feature of the scoring to investigate, since the scores are tracking area rather than the written descriptors.
Accept the relationship as a genuine finding, since it holds across all twenty schemes.
options.misconception: treats a scoring pattern as a discovered truth about gardens

options.text: Remove the area information from the notes, so that the panel is not influenced by it.
options.misconception: removes the record that would explain the pattern

options.text: Add an area criterion to the matrix, so the panel scores garden size directly in future.
options.misconception: codifies an artefact as a criterion

questions.explanation: When scores track one physical variable across every case, the descriptors or the markers' assumptions are doing the work rather than the text. The relationship is a signal to investigate, and a basis for a finding, but it is not yet a finding about landscape quality.
questions.hint: Ask whether the descriptors mention area at all.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion and the observable behind it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the observable behind a stated criterion
questions.stem: A memo lists 'appropriateness of the housing mix to local need' as a criterion, and the panel asks what would show a submission meeting it.

options.text: Ask the applicant to state that the mix was chosen to meet local need in the area.
options.misconception: accepts a claim where an observable is needed

options.text: Ask for evidence against the local need figure, such as the unit sizes compared with neighbourhood data.
Ask the applicant to show a good mix of house types, which is what local need means.
options.misconception: substitutes a general quality for a specific comparison

options.text: Ask the panel to compare the mix with what it saw on the last site visit to the area.
options.misconception: uses an impression from one visit as the evidence

questions.explanation: A criterion about local need is only checkable against a stated local need figure, so the submission's unit sizes have to be compared with the neighbourhood data. A declaration, a general notion of a good mix, or a panel's memory each substitute something else for the comparison.
questions.hint: Ask what the mix has to be compared against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rubric level describes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a rubric level actually specifies

stimulus.body: A panel's rubric has four bands for the criterion 'street tree provision': 'none, some, good, generous'. Two markers gave the same scheme a 'good' rating and wrote the same sentence about the trees.

questions.stem: What does the matching band and the matching sentence tell the officer?

options.text: The band is performing as intended, since both markers saw the same trees and reached the same place.
options.misconception: confuses agreement with a shared description

options.text: The band is too coarse, because a four-point scale can never be applied reliably.
options.misconception: blames the scale rather than the missing description

options.text: The band carries no description, so the agreement came from a shared impression rather than from the rubric.
The markers need retraining, since they should know what good tree provision means.
options.misconception: assigns the failure to the markers instead of the rubric

questions.explanation: Two markers can agree by sharing an impression of the same trees, and agreement of that kind tells the officer nothing about whether the band is doing work. The band needs to say what provision places a scheme in it before agreement means anything.
questions.hint: Ask what the band tells a marker to look for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Improvement as the thing being marked
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish improvement from mere compliance in marking
questions.stem: A city reopens a pedestrianised street scheme and the memo asks the panel to judge whether the reworking represents an improvement on the earlier arrangement.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say judging improvement requires the earlier arrangement to be described in comparable terms, including what the street was like for walking, for deliveries and for the shops that front it. Without that description the panel is left comparing a remembered impression with a drawn scheme, and the judgment becomes a preference between two things rather than a measurement of change against a stated starting point.

questions.explanation: Improvement can only be judged against a stated starting point, so the earlier arrangement has to be described in comparable terms. Comparing a memory with a drawing produces a preference rather than a finding about change.
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier arrangement was like, in writing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet
questions.stem: A brief awards marks for a development that contains no vehicle parking, and the officer confirms the scheme requires at least one accessible space per dwelling.

options.text: Award the marks to the application with the smallest parking provision, as the closest available to the requirement.
options.misconception: substitutes a near miss for a criterion that cannot be met

options.text: Leave the marks unclaimed across the batch, since the requirement is plainly not satisfiable.
options.misconception: leaves a defect in the marks unexplained to readers

options.text: Award the marks to all applications equally, so that no plot size is favoured.
options.misconception: spreads a defective criterion so that nobody is penalised

options.text: Record the criterion as unmeetable, report its effect on the ranking and refer the wording for correction.

questions.explanation: An unmeetable criterion awards nothing and redistributes the effective weight of everything else, so the officer's duty is to record it, show the effect and refer the wording back. Substituting a near miss, an equal award or a silent blank each produces a score the framework does not describe.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the other criteria when this one is applied.

questions.stem: A panel's checklist includes 'whether the applicant has paid the required fee', and every application in the batch has paid.

options.misconception: keeps a procedural item inside the scored assessment

options.text: Award it only to applicants who paid early, to reward promptness with the city.
options.misconception: invents a timing rule to make the item discriminate

options.text: Award it to none, since paying a fee is not a design achievement in any case.
options.misconception: reads a procedural item as if it were a quality judgement

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: Work out what a set of weightings rewards
questions.stem: A matrix gives 5 per cent to 'conserving heritage', 25 per cent to 'public transport' and 70 per cent to 'design quality', and the chair asks what follows from that arrangement.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the matrix is a statement of priorities, and with 70 per cent on design a scheme that is weak on transport and heritage can still be recommended if its design is strong. That is a legitimate political choice, but it has to be made openly and defended as such, because applicants reading the matrix will invest their effort in the heaviest weights, and the panel's informal judgements will be quietly overridden by the totals.

questions.explanation: Weightings are priorities expressed in marks, so they decide outcomes that an unweighted discussion might treat as equal. Making the priority explicit lets the committee defend it and lets applicants aim their effort accordingly.
questions.hint: Ask which criterion a weak scheme can compensate for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Self-assessment without a shared reference point
questions.learningObjective: Explain why self-assessment needs a shared reference point

stimulus.body: An officer asks four applicant teams to self-score the same code. The teams' self-scores range from 55 to 90 per cent. Each team separately cites a different worked example from its own precedents to justify its rating.

questions.stem: What should the officer do with the four self-scores?

options.text: Average the four scores, so that the average team receives the average rating.
options.misconception: averages away the absence of a shared reference

options.text: Treat the spread as uninformative about quality and calibrate the teams against a common worked example.
Use the median of the four scores, since the median resists the most generous team.
options.misconception: thinks a robust average creates a shared standard

options.text: Discard the lowest score as an outlier and work with the remaining three figures.
options.misconception: treats a miscalibrated reading as a data error to remove

questions.explanation: Each team rated against its own precedent, so the spread measures the differences in their references rather than in the scheme. Averaging, taking the median or dropping the lowest figure all produce a number with no standard behind it.
questions.hint: Ask what each team used as its reference point.

questions.topic: Scores that follow a relationship rather than a text
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a score that tracks a relationship rather than a text

options.text: Accept the ordering, since more experience should produce better responses to the street.
options.misconception: accepts a scoring artefact as a measure of experience

options.text: Accept the ordering, since the codes and the panel membership were the same throughout the period.
options.misconception: treats a constant framework as proof of a constant measurement

options.text: Treat the pattern as a question about the panel's practice, since the score is tracking completion date rather than the text.
Reweight the criterion to remove the trend, so that future schemes are scored consistently.
options.misconception: corrects a possible artefact by adding a weighting

questions.explanation: A score that rises in step with a date is tracking something other than the descriptors, and a constant framework does not protect against a drift in how markers read it. The panel needs to ask what it has been rewarding over those years before the scores are used.

questions.topic: What a rubric level describes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a rubric level actually specifies
questions.stem: A rubric for the criterion 'materials' has a band described as 'durable but generic', and the officer asks what a marker should conclude from it.

options.text: That the scheme performs adequately on materials without meeting the standard the city is looking for.
That the scheme has chosen the wrong materials and should be refused at this stage.
options.misconception: reads a moderate band as a refusal trigger

options.text: That the band tells the marker how many marks to award for the materials criterion.
options.misconception: confuses a band description with the score attached to it

options.text: That the band applies to the whole application rather than to the materials criterion alone.
options.misconception: widens the scope of a single band beyond its criterion

questions.explanation: A band description states how the scheme performs on that criterion, and 'durable but generic' places the scheme in the middle rather than at the top or the bottom. It does not carry a mark, trigger a refusal or reach beyond its own criterion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Improvement as the thing being marked
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish improvement from mere compliance in marking
questions.stem: A city compares a new bus shelter design with the one it replaced, and the memo asks whether the new design should be marked as an improvement.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say marking improvement requires the replaced shelter to be described in the same terms the new one will be assessed, such as capacity in the peak hour, shelter from wind and rain, and how long passengers wait without a seat. Without that description the panel is being asked for a preference, and a preference dressed up as an improvement measure will track whoever presented the case rather than the design's actual qualities.

questions.explanation: A comparison of old and new needs both described in the same terms, otherwise the judgment becomes a preference. Specifying the comparable features is what makes the improvement claim a measurement rather than an opinion.
questions.hint: Ask what the replaced shelter provided, in figures.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet

stimulus.body: A committee paper scores 'a contribution of at least 400 square metres of new public open space within the site boundary'. The 19 applications in the batch have site boundaries that make 400 square metres impossible on all but one.

questions.stem: The committee asks how the criterion should be handled in this batch.

options.text: Award the marks to the one application that can meet the threshold, since the criterion does work there.
options.misconception: keeps a defective criterion because one case happens to meet it

options.text: Report the criterion as unmeetable for most of the batch and give the committee the effect on the ranking.
Scale the threshold down for each application in proportion to the size of its site.
options.misconception: invents a site-specific rule the published criterion does not contain

options.text: Award the marks to the application with the largest open space, as the closest effort to the target.
options.misconception: turns a threshold into a ranking of effort

questions.explanation: A threshold that almost no application can reach cannot separate the batch, and its weight falls on the criteria that can. Reporting the defect and its effect before the scores are published keeps the committee's decision based on a ranking it understands.
questions.hint: Ask what the criterion contributes to the ranking in this batch.

questions.topic: A criterion every submission meets
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that every submission meets
questions.stem: A scoring sheet has a row confirming that each application was submitted before the deadline, and all 22 submissions arrived in time.

options.text: Award the marks to all 22, since the deadline is a rule the city set for everyone.
options.misconception: keeps a non-discriminating item in the scored assessment

options.text: Award the marks to the earliest submissions, so that punctuality is rewarded with points.
options.misconception: invents a ranking rule the city never set

options.text: Mark the row as met by all and leave it out of the scored total, since it cannot tell the submissions apart.
Award the marks to none, since arriving on time is a rule rather than a design achievement.
options.misconception: treats a met procedural item as an unearned mark

questions.explanation: A punctuality row that everyone satisfies adds the same marks to every total and informs no decision about quality. Recording it as met and leaving it out of the scored total keeps the published ranking a ranking of the submissions themselves.

questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: Work out what a set of weightings rewards
questions.stem: A committee wants to change a matrix in which design holds 70 per cent of the marks and affordable housing 30 per cent, and the chair asks for a defensible way to decide.

options.text: Ask the panel members to state which weight they prefer, and use the average of their preferences.
options.misconception: treats a vote on weights as though it settled the priority

options.text: Keep the current weights, since they have been used for three review cycles already.
options.misconception: mistakes continuity for justification

options.text: Set the weights by what similar councils use, so the city is consistent with its peers.
options.misconception: borrows a weighting without evidence about the local case

options.text: State the policy priority the change expresses, then set the weights that follow from it and record why.

questions.explanation: A weighting is a policy choice, so it needs a policy reason on the record, and the reason has to be checked against the effect on the schemes already assessed. Voting, inertia and borrowed figures can each produce a number without producing a defensible priority.
questions.hint: Ask what the change is meant to achieve in the city.

options.text: Expect the self-scores to reflect each applicant's own reading, and add calibration before the panel uses them.
Expect the self-scores to be unreliable, and simply ignore them when the panel scores.
options.misconception: discards a source that calibration could make useful

options.text: Expect the self-scores to be roughly right, since applicants know their own schemes best.
options.misconception: assumes self-knowledge substitutes for a shared standard

options.text: Expect the self-scores to vary, and average them to get a fair figure for each scheme.
options.misconception: averages away the absence of a shared reference point

questions.explanation: Without a worked example each applicant applies its own idea of the bands, so the spread measures reading rather than quality. Calibration is what turns the self-scores into something the panel can use, and it does not require discarding them.

questions.explanation: A relationship that holds across every case may be the measurement showing through rather than a fact about the schemes. Checking the descriptors and the markers' assumptions tells the officer which of the two she is looking at.

options.text: A letter confirming that the scheme is in accordance with the local plan as adopted.
options.misconception: accepts a statement of compliance as the evidence

options.text: A costed housing schedule setting the affordable units against the plan's required number and rents.
An officer's certificate that the scheme meets the plan, attached after the assessment is done.
options.misconception: uses a later certificate to stand in for the submission

options.text: A comparison with the affordable housing delivered by the two most recent approvals in the city.
options.misconception: substitutes a precedent for the submission's own evidence

questions.explanation: The criterion asks for a response to a stated requirement, so the observable is the submission's own schedule set against that requirement. A compliance letter, a later certificate and a precedent each answer a different question and none of them is the submission's response.

options.text: Clear marks attached to each band, so that the panel can total the sheet quickly at the end.
options.misconception: makes a band a score rather than a description

options.text: A statement of who wrote the rubric, so that the panel knows whose judgement it is applying.
options.misconception: treats authorship as the substance of a band

options.text: Descriptions of what a submission looks like at each band, in terms a marker can recognise on a drawing.
An instruction to split the difference whenever markers disagree about which band applies.
options.misconception: uses a rule about disagreement in place of band descriptions

questions.stem: A city reworks a market square and asks the panel to judge whether the reworking improves on the old square, but only the new square has been measured.

options.text: Ask residents whether the square feels better than the old one was, and report their view.
options.misconception: uses a preference poll in place of a comparison of measures

options.text: Compare the two squares on the cost of the works, which the city has recorded for both.
options.misconception: uses cost as a proxy for the quality of the space

options.text: Judge the new square on its own merits, since the old square was widely criticised already.
options.misconception: lets a prior reputation stand in for a baseline

questions.stem: A panel's notes show that the two schemes with the longest consultation responses received the highest design scores, and the officer asks what to make of it.

options.text: Treat it as a pattern to investigate, since a score should follow the descriptors rather than the volume of correspondence.
Accept the link, since a well-argued response usually means a better thought-through design.
options.misconception: accepts a correlation between correspondence and quality as a cause

options.misconception: hides the pattern instead of testing it

options.misconception: responds to a possible artefact by changing the weights

questions.explanation: A score that follows the length of the correspondence is tracking something the criterion does not mention, which is a warning about the scoring rather than a finding about design. Testing the descriptors and the markers' habits is what distinguishes the two.

questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet
questions.stem: An assessment framework awards marks for the design of a public bridge, and the framework applies to a batch of small housing sites on which no bridge could ever be built.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a criterion that cannot apply to any case in the batch awards nobody anything and shifts the effective weight of every other criterion, so the final ranking is not the one the framework describes. The defensible course is to record the mismatch, publish the scores with an explanation of what the criterion did and did not do, and refer the framework wording to be amended before it is applied to the next batch.

questions.explanation: A criterion that applies to no case in the batch awards nothing and quietly redistributes the marks, so the ranking is not what the framework says it is. Recording and reporting the mismatch keeps the published scores honest.
questions.hint: Ask what the criterion does to the weight of the others.

options.text: Award the marks to all nine, since ownership is a material factor in the assessment of the site.
options.misconception: keeps a met item in the scored total because the subject matters

options.text: Record it as satisfied by all and leave it out of the scored total, keeping it as a compliance check.
Award the marks to the applications with the longest ownership histories among the nine.
options.misconception: invents an extra test to make the row discriminate

options.text: Cross the row out of the sheet before scoring, so that the panel concentrates on design.
options.misconception: removes a compliance step from the assessment

questions.explanation: The row has a stated purpose as a compliance trigger, and because every applicant satisfies it it has no power to separate them. Keeping it out of the scored total and as a check preserves its function without inflating the published scores.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: Work out what a set of weightings rewards
questions.stem: A matrix awards 40 per cent to transport, 40 per cent to design and 20 per cent to community benefit, and the officer asks what happens when a scheme is weak on one criterion.

options.text: Every criterion must be met, since equal weights mean equal importance in every case.
options.misconception: assumes weights and minimum standards are the same thing

options.text: The panel should average the criteria that matter to it and disregard the rest of the matrix.
options.misconception: lets each marker substitute personal criteria for the matrix

options.text: A scheme strong on two criteria can still score highly, so weakness in one area is tolerated unless a minimum is set.
The scheme will fail automatically, because a weak criterion cancels out a strong one.
options.misconception: invents a rule that the matrix does not contain

questions.explanation: A matrix of weights compensates, so a scheme can be strong overall while weak on one criterion, unless the framework also sets a minimum for that criterion. A compensation rule or a cancellation rule is a separate decision that has to be made explicitly.
questions.hint: Ask whether the matrix sets a floor as well as a weight.

options.text: Collect the self-ratings and use the average as the starting point for the panel's discussion of fit.
options.misconception: averages away the missing reference point

options.text: Ask each team to bring an example of a scheme it considers a good fit, and use those as the reference.
options.misconception: lets each team set its own standard

options.text: Skip the self-assessment step, since the panel will form its own view of fit in any case.
options.misconception: discards a source that calibration could make useful

options.text: Produce a worked example judged by the panel, show it to the teams and only then collect the self-ratings.

questions.explanation: A worked example judged by the panel gives the teams a reference point in common, which is the only thing that makes their ratings comparable with the panel's own. Team-chosen examples leave each team where it started, and averaging leaves the same problem in place.

options.text: A criterion should name the number of marks available, so that the panel can total the sheet quickly.
options.misconception: confuses a criterion with a scoring band

options.text: A criterion should name the document the applicant must supply, so that the files are complete.
options.misconception: confuses a criterion with a submission requirement

questions.learningObjective: Describe what a rubric level actually specifies
questions.stem: A panel asks what should distinguish the band 'adequate' from the band 'good' on the criterion 'accessibility', and the officer has to answer.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the two bands have to differ in the observable features of the submission, such as the gradient and width of the route, the presence of a dropped kerb, and how a level change is handled. options.text: Judging improvement means asking residents whether they prefer the new park to the old one.
options.misconception: substitutes preference for a comparison of conditions

questions.explanation: Improvement is a difference between two conditions, so both have to be described on the same measures for the difference to mean anything. A bonus for being a replacement, a rule that guarantees the higher score and a preference poll each answer a different question.
questions.hint: Ask what is being compared with what.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet

stimulus.body: A scoring guide gives marks for a 'seaward viewing platform'. The batch of 8 applications consists of inland sites 40 miles from the coast, and the officer confirms that no seaward frontage is possible anywhere in the batch.

questions.stem: What does the officer need to put in the report to the committee?

options.text: Nothing, since the guide will award no marks and the ranking will be unaffected by the gap.
options.misconception: assumes an unmeetable criterion has no effect on the ranking

options.text: A note that the criterion could not be met by any application, what that did to the weights and a referral to correct the wording.
A revised score sheet for this batch with the criterion removed, circulated before the meeting.
options.misconception: changes the assessment instrument without recording the change

options.text: A recommendation that the batch be assessed on a different guide, since this one does not fit.
options.misconception: abandons the whole framework over one defective row

questions.explanation: The committee has to know that a row in the guide awarded nothing and what that did to the marks that did count, otherwise the published ranking cannot be read against the guide. Correcting the wording is what stops the same defect appearing in the next batch.
questions.hint: Ask what the committee needs to know about the guide's effect.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion every submission meets
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that every submission meets
questions.stem: A committee's assessment has a criterion for 'the extent to which the scheme is accessible by public transport', and every application in the batch sits within 400 metres of a bus stop.

options.text: The criterion cannot separate the applications in this batch, so it is recorded as met by all rather than treated as a differentiator.
The criterion separates the applications, because proximity to a stop still varies between them.
options.misconception: treats a narrow range of performance as meaningful discrimination

options.text: The criterion is invalid, because the city has no authority to assess transport access at all.
options.misconception: attacks the criterion's legitimacy rather than its discriminating power

options.text: The criterion should be dropped from the framework, since it never fails to be met.
options.misconception: removes a criterion for being met rather than for being unusable

questions.explanation: A criterion met by every application cannot rank them, whatever the range within the band, and treating it as a differentiator gives the panel a false sense of discrimination. Removing it from the framework is a separate decision from recording that it did no work in this batch.
questions.hint: Ask what the criterion would tell the committee about the ranking.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: Work out what a set of weightings rewards
questions.stem: A committee proposes raising the weight on affordable housing from 20 to 40 per cent, and the chair asks what should be checked before the change is made.

options.text: Whether the panel has enough time to discuss the newly weighted criterion in the meeting itself.
options.misconception: treats meeting time as the decisive factor

options.text: Whether the applicants will complain, since a change of weights affects the schemes they design.
options.misconception: makes applicant reaction the test for a policy choice

options.text: Whether the current weight matches the share of affordable units in the recent approvals in the city.
options.misconception: derives a policy weight from historical outcomes

options.text: Whether the change expresses a stated policy priority, and what it does to the schemes already assessed.

questions.explanation: A weight is a policy priority, so the reason for changing it has to be stated, and the effect on the schemes already scored has to be known before the committee commits. Time, complaints and historical shares are all considerations, none of which is the justification.
questions.hint: Ask what the change is meant to achieve and what it does to current scores.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Self-assessment without a shared reference point
questions.learningObjective: Explain why self-assessment needs a shared reference point
questions.stem: A planning committee asks teams to self-score their schemes against a code, and the officer notes that every team has scored its own scheme in the highest band.

options.text: Treat the exercise as showing little about the schemes, because without a shared reference the bands mean whatever each team takes them to mean.
Treat the exercise as showing that the schemes are all of the same high standard on the code.
options.misconception: reads a common self-rating as a common quality

options.text: Treat the exercise as a way of identifying the schemes that need the most scrutiny from the panel.
options.misconception: reads a self-rating as a needs assessment

options.text: Treat the exercise as a useful ranking of the teams by their own standards, which tells the officer a lot.
options.misconception: treats the spread of standards as a ranking of teams

questions.explanation: When every team puts its own scheme in the top band, the useful reading is that the bands mean different things to each team, not that the schemes are equivalent. Without a shared reference the exercise cannot speak about quality at all.
questions.hint: Ask what every team's rating is evidence of.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Scores that follow a relationship rather than a text
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a score that tracks a relationship rather than a text
questions.stem: An officer finds that panel scores for 'quality of the shopfront design' rise in near-perfect proportion to the number of shopfronts drawn on the elevations, across 21 schemes.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a relationship this exact across every scheme is more likely to be the measurement showing through than a fact about design, because markers do not normally compute a ratio while scoring. The officer should read the descriptors to see whether drawing more shopfronts is rewarded in words, and should ask markers whether they are applying an unstated assumption that more shopfronts mean a more active street.

questions.explanation: A near-perfect relationship across cases points at the descriptors or the markers' assumptions rather than at a discovery about design. Reading the wording and asking the panel is what distinguishes the two possibilities.
questions.hint: Ask why the number of drawn shopfronts would matter to a score.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion and the observable behind it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the observable behind a stated criterion
questions.stem: A planning memo's criteria cover design quality, transport impact and community benefit, and the officer is asked why each criterion should name an observable.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say a criterion that names an observable can be applied to whatever the applicant submits, whether that is a drawing, a schedule or a statement, and two markers applying it can be expected to arrive at the same reading. A criterion that names only a quality invites each marker to supply their own standard, which makes the score a record of the panel's preferences rather than of the submission.

questions.explanation: A criterion that points to something checkable can be applied consistently across different submissions and different markers. One that names only a quality leaves the standard to each reader.
questions.hint: Ask what two markers would each supply for themselves.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rubric level describes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a rubric level actually specifies

stimulus.body: A panel's rubric for the criterion 'play space' has three bands: 'none provided', 'some provision' and 'well provided'. Two markers independently rated the same scheme 'some provision' and their notes both say the scheme has a small play area near the flats.

questions.stem: What does the band set need in order to work in practice?

options.text: A fourth band, so that panels have room to distinguish between stronger schemes.
options.misconception: believes more bands will fix a description problem

options.text: Descriptions of what the higher bands require, so that 'some' and 'well' apply to a scheme the same way.
A rule about how markers should split the difference when they disagree about a band.
options.misconception: answers a disagreement problem with a description gap

options.text: Training for markers, since the problem is that the panels are inexperienced in play space.
options.misconception: blames the markers for what the rubric omits

questions.explanation: The bands have names but no content, so 'some' and 'well' depend on each marker supplying a threshold of their own. Describing what each higher band requires is what makes the two markers' agreement meaningful rather than coincidental.
questions.hint: Ask what the higher band actually asks the marker to find.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Improvement as the thing being marked
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish improvement from mere compliance in marking
questions.stem: A city compares a new park design with the old one and finds the new scheme has more trees, more seating and a longer opening hour, and the officer asks what the memo should conclude.

options.text: The new park is better on every measure the city could check, so the panel can award the improvement rating.
options.misconception: treats a partial set of measures as a complete comparison

options.text: The new park is better on trees, seating and hours, but the memo does not yet say what the old park had that was lost.
options.misconception: draws a total judgment from a partial record without noting its limit

options.text: The improvement is established on the three measured features, and the memo should say which other qualities were not compared.
The comparison tells the panel little, since the old park was designed for a different era of the city.
options.misconception: dismisses usable evidence because the baseline has changed

questions.explanation: Three measured features support an improvement claim on those features, and the memo has to say so without implying that the whole case has been made. Naming the qualities that were not compared is what keeps the conclusion at the level of the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the memo has not measured yet.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a criterion that no submission can meet
questions.stem: A framework awards marks for the design of a new footbridge, and the batch of 11 applications is for small infill sites where the planning authority has already ruled that no bridge is possible.

options.text: Award the marks to whichever application makes the strongest case for a bridge in its design statement.
options.misconception: scores the strength of an argument about an unmeetable criterion

options.text: Award no marks for the criterion and note on the score sheet that it was not assessable in this batch.
options.misconception: records nothing about the effect on the ranking

options.text: Award the marks to the scheme that would need the fewest people to use a bridge if one were built.
options.misconception: invents a proxy test to keep a criterion alive

options.text: Record the criterion as unassessable for this batch, report its effect on the weights and refer the wording.

questions.explanation: A criterion the authority has already ruled out cannot be scored for any application, so the officer has to record that, show what its weight did to the totals and refer the wording for correction. Scoring arguments, leaving a silent blank and inventing proxies all produce results the framework does not describe.
questions.hint: Ask what the committee needs to know about the marks awarded.
